summary: A slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 700 through RFC 799, serving as a status report on them. It is a handy index to that stretch of the series.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 800 is a catalogue of the hundred RFCs numbered 700 to 799, written in 1982. For each one it gives the author, the date, the title and a short note, and it points out which later document replaced it.

subtitle: A short, annotated list of a hundred RFCs, with a note on each one.

tldr.problem: The RFC series grows one document at a time, and early documents were often replaced by later ones without the reader being told. By 1982 the list of the first few hundred RFCs was hard to navigate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 800 is a status report on the hundred RFCs numbered 700 to 799. Each entry gives the number, the author, the date, the title and a sentence or two saying what the document was and, where it applies, what later document replaced it.
tldr.outcome: The list covers the founding specifications of the Internet's core protocols, the early mail and file transfer work, the first attempts at a hierarchical name system, and a long run of Assigned Numbers updates. It is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A Status Report on a Hundred RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 800 is a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 700 through RFC 799. The RFC calls itself a kind of status report on these RFCs, and it was written by Jon Postel and Joyce Vernon at ISI in November 1982.

The purpose it serves is simple. By 1982 the series already had a long tail of documents that had been quietly replaced by newer ones. An Assigned Numbers memorandum, for instance, appeared in many versions, and the early versions of the core protocol specifications had all been superseded. A reader who picked up an old RFC had no way of telling whether it was still the current statement of the protocol or not, so the list answers that question in a line for each entry.

The material covered by these hundred documents is broad. It includes the founding specifications of the Internet itself and of the protocols that ran over it, the first work on electronic mail, the beginnings of a name system, a long series of Telnet options, and a great deal of housekeeping about assigned numbers. The list also captures a period when the protocols were still being designed rather than merely documented, with several entries describing proposals and surveys rather than final specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The list was written so that a reader holding an old document could tell at a glance whether it still mattered. For most entries the answer is a pointer to the document that replaced it.

sections.title: The Shape of Each Entry
sections.content:
Every entry has the same four-part header line: the RFC number, the author's name, the date, and the title. Beneath that is a short annotation, usually one or two sentences, saying what the document contains.

The header lines are set out in columns, with the RFC number first, then the author, then the date, and then the title, which wraps where it is long. The dates are given in the compact form of the period, with a two-digit year, so RFC 793 is dated Sep 81 and RFC 700 is dated Aug 74.

The annotations are written as descriptions rather than as reviews. For example, the entry for RFC 797, Format for Bitmap Files, reads that it is the description of a simple file format for bitmap data. The entry for RFC 787, Connectionless Data Transmission Survey/Tutorial, notes that it is a discussion of the datagram service intended for submission to international standards bodies. Where a document has a particular standing, the annotation says so: RFC 778, DCNet Internet Clock Service, specifies a format and procedure for exchanging messages to keep clocks synchronised, and RFC 785 through RFC 784 are each marked as describing the ISI TOPS20 mail transfer program and are marked outdated.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry looks the same: number, author, date, title, and a sentence about what is inside. The wording is plain, and it is meant to be read quickly rather than studied.

sections.title: What the Hundred RFCs Were About
sections.content:
The most important documents in the list are the specifications of the protocols the Internet is built on, and the entries make that clear. RFC 791 is the Internet Protocol, replacing RFC 760. RFC 793 is the Transmission Control Protocol, replacing RFCs 761 and 675. RFC 792 is the Internet Control Message Protocol, replacing RFCs 777 and 760. RFC 768 is the User Datagram Protocol. RFC 765 is the File Transfer Protocol and RFC 764 is the Telnet Protocol Specification.

Mail occupies a large part of the list, and it shows the protocol settling down. RFC 733 and RFC 724 are earlier versions of the format for computer mail headers, and both are annotated as old versions of RFC 822. RFC 772, RFC 780 and RFC 788 are earlier mail transfer protocols, all pointed at RFC 821. Several documents in the 780s describe the ISI TOPS20 mail transfer implementation in detail and are marked outdated.

Names and addresses get their own thread. RFC 799 suggests that as the Internet grows, host names cannot remain a flat space of globally unique names and that a hierarchy of name domains should be introduced. RFC 756 describes a host name to address lookup service, RFC 752 describes the host table used at MIT and Stanford, and RFC 799 and RFC 757 both discuss ways of getting from a name to an address.

Two entries are worth singling out because they read as warnings rather than specifications. RFC 789 describes an outage in ARPANET service and the process of determining the cause, along with subtleties in designing network protocols. RFC 706 points out that the ARPANET might be subject to a denial of service attack by a misbehaving host, and RFC 728 warns of an unexpected occurrence in Telnet resulting from the interaction between option subnegotiations and the SYNCH operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The list covers the protocols everyone uses, the mail and file transfer systems of the time, the first attempts to give the Internet a hierarchy of names, and a few notes from the operating incidents that shaped later design.

sections.title: How the List Tracks Supersession
sections.content:
The annotations carry the status information, and they use a small set of repeated phrases.

An entry that has been replaced by a later document reads as an old version and points to the newer number. RFC 776 is an old version and the entry says to see RFC 790. RFC 777 is an old version and the entry says to see RFC 792. RFC 761 is an old version and the entry says to see RFC 793. This phrase is used for a long run of the Assigned Numbers memoranda, from RFC 758 and RFC 755 through RFC 750 and RFC 739, and also for the early versions of the mail and message formats.

The newer document points back. RFC 790, the Assigned Numbers memorandum, says that it replaces RFCs 776, 770, 762, 758, 755, 750, 739 and 604. RFC 791 replaces RFC 760, RFC 792 replaces RFCs 777 and 760, and RFC 793 replaces RFCs 761 and 675.

Three other phrasings appear. A document that has been absorbed into a later protocol is described as now incorporated into it: the FTP mail extension in RFC 743 is now incorporated into SMTP, and the FTP extension XSEN in RFC 737 is incorporated in SMTP. A document that is simply gone is marked outdated, as with the ISI TOPS20 mail transfer documents. And a see also phrase points at a related document without saying which one replaced which, as with RFC 757, which points at RFCs 759, 821 and 822, and RFC 799, which points at RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: The status is in the wording. An old document says so and names the replacement; the replacement names the documents it took over from. A few entries are marked outdated or point sideways to something related.

sections.title: What the List Still Shows
sections.content:
Read as a whole, the list is a snapshot of the Internet at a particular moment. The dates run from Aug 74, when RFC 700 describes a protocol experiment loosely based on a very early version of TCP and used to send data to a printer server, through to Sep 81, when RFC 793 and RFC 792 were written. The intervening years show the protocol suite being written down, replaced and written down again.

Several entries are about the design process rather than a finished protocol. RFC 714 specifies a host-to-host protocol for an ARPANET-like network and is noted as interesting to compare with the NCP specification to see what the author would do differently. RFC 722 discusses the design of interactive distributed services and the kinds of primitive operations needed. RFC 703, 702 and 701 are successive surveys of new-protocol Telnet servers, each checking implementation status and Telnet options, and each pointing at the ones before it.

The housekeeping entries fill much of the list. Assigned Numbers was reissued many times, each version naming the ones it replaced, and the list is the clearest single view of how often that happened. The remaining entries cover terminal options and protocols for specific host systems, facsimile formats, a database service for computer mail messages, and a set of remote job entry protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Taken together the entries are a record of the Internet being designed rather than just written down, with the housekeeping of assigned numbers running through the whole thing.
